sec.title: Experimental model and study participant details
Patient samples and clinical data collection
sec.p: This study included 45 longitudinal tumor specimens collected from 10 patients (4 Rs and 6 NRs to anti-PD-1 therapy). Patient MP13_674 provided written informed consent for biospecimen collection and data usage under the University of Pennsylvania Abramson Cancer Center’s melanoma research program tissue collection protocol (IRB#703001), which was approved by the Institutional Review Board (IRB) of the University of Pennsylvania. The protocol was further reviewed and approved by the Clinical Trials Scientific Review and Monitoring Committee (CTSRMC) and the Data and Safety Monitoring Committee (DSMC) at the Abramson Cancer Center (UPCC# 08607). Additionally, patient G001, who underwent treatment at Duke University, provided written informed consent for biospecimen collection, medical record review, and publication of the data, in accordance with IRB protocols (IRB# Pro00086652 and Pro00090678). Six additional patients (Pt35, Pt42, Pt208, Pt272, Pt530, Pt98) from Massachusetts General Hospital (MGH) were enrolled in the study, with tumor specimens collected at pre-treatment, on-treatment, and/or post-treatment time points, and data from MGH Pt98 was sourced from a previously published study.37,42 All patients provided informed consent, and the study adhered to the ethical guidelines specified in the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute IRB protocol (11–181) and The Wistar Institute Human Subjects protocol (2802240). Furthermore, patients S001 and S002 were enrolled from Sun Yat-sen University Cancer Center (SYSUCC), with biospecimen collection and data usage conducted under the IRB protocol of SYSUCC (Protocol B2021-256-01), which was approved by the Medical Ethics Committee of SYSUCC. Written informed consent was obtained from all patients.

Detailed demographic information regarding biological gender, age at diagnosis and disease stage for these participants is provided in Table S1. Data regarding ancestry, race, ethnicity, and socioeconomic status were not collected for this retrospective cohort. Due to the limited sample size, statistical analysis regarding the influence of biological gender on the experimental results was not performed.

Rs were defined as patients achieving a complete response (CR), partial response (PR), or stable disease (SD) with progression-free survival (PFS) exceeding 180 days. Conversely, NRs were those with progressive disease (PD) or SD with a PFS of less than 180 days.41 For Patient G001, who participated in multiple clinical trials, response assessment followed trial-specific protocols. RECIST 1.1 was used during the Ipi plus Nivolumab and subsequent Pembrolizumab plus SD-101 treatments (NCT02521870), while immune-related Response Criteria (irRC) were applied during the Pembrolizumab plus T-VEC therapy (NCT03712358). The clinical responses of the remaining nine patients were evaluated using RECIST 1.1. Patient G001 demonstrated progression of disease under the Pembrolizumab plus T-VEC regimen according to irRC, characterized by a >25% increase in tumor burden.88 Since this clinical presentation also met the criteria for PD under RECIST 1.1, Patient G001 was classified as an NR and included in the pooled analysis alongside the other patients.89 PFS was defined as the time from the start of treatment to the date of first documented disease progression or death from any cause, whichever occurred first. OS was defined as the time from the start of treatment to the date of death from any cause.

sec.title: Validation cohorts from published data
sec.p: To validate the PI3K pathway alterations, we established an external cohort consisting of RNA-seq data from 19 paired pre-treatment and post-anti-PD-1/L1 treatment metastatic melanoma samples aggregated from previously published studies: 1) Lee et al. (EGA accession number EGAD00001005738)38; 2) Johnson et al. (RNA-seq data obtained from the corresponding author)39; 3) Wei et al.,40 Du et al.41 and Auslander et al.42 (GSE168204, GSE115821, GSE273583).

To validate the mTOR signaling and RCN3 architectural signatures, we analyzed data from independent external cohorts comprising both single-cell and bulk transcriptomic datasets. Single-cell transcriptomic data include: 1) Yang et al. (scRNA-seq, GSE269936)32; and 2) Quek et al. (Mendeley Data, https://doi.org/10.17632/w55dvbb82f.1).33 For clinical outcome and survival analyses, we utilized bulk RNA-seq and clinical data from: 3) Du et al. and Auslander et al. (GSE168204 and GSE115821)41,42; 4) Riaz et al. (GSE91061)57; 5) Gide et al. (PRJEB23709)58; and 6) TCGA-SKCM dataset (obtained from the GDC Data Portal).36 While basic demographic data such as biological gender and age were available for specific samples within these cohorts, comprehensive information regarding gender identity, ancestry, race, ethnicity, and socioeconomic status was not uniformly collected or reportable across the aggregated datasets.

sec.title: DNA and RNA extraction
sec.p: Formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded (FFPE) and/or frozen tumor samples were obtained via surgical resection or core biopsy (18G) of metastatic lesions, as per clinical standard for managing progressive metastatic melanoma. Each time point sampled distinct metastatic sites (e.g., brain, lymph node, subcutaneous), to capture tumor evolution under therapy. Tumor samples were used for subsequent analyses, including WES, RNA-seq, DSP, CyCIF, mIHC and 10x Genomics Visium HD. FFPE tumor tissues were fixed in 10% formalin, embedded in paraffin, and serially sectioned. H&E staining of FFPE slides was performed using standard histological techniques. Additionally, frozen tissue samples were prepared for RPPA and RNA-seq.

For patients MP13_674 and G001, DNA/RNA co-purification was processed using AllPrep DNA/RNA FFPE Kit (Cat# 80234, Qiagen; Germantown, MD, USA) or GenElute FFPE RNA/DNA Purification Plus Kit (Cat# Rdp200, Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA) according to manufacturers’ instructions. Briefly, 50μm sections were transferred into a 2mL tube and deparaffinization was performed by adding 1mL xylene with an incubation at 50°C for 5m followed by centrifugation. Supernatants were aspirated and 96–100% ethanol was added followed by centrifugation to remove any residual xylene. Pellets were dried at 37°C before continuing column-based purification procedures. RNaseA or DNase I treatment was added during DNA or RNA purification, respectively. RNA and DNA were eluted in DNase/RNase free water separately and quantified with Qubit 3.0 Qubit dsDNA HS Assay kit (Cat# Q32851) and/or RNA HS Assay kit (Cat# Q10210) (Life Technologies; Carlsbad, CA, USA) according to recommended protocols. Only FFPE samples with a DV200 score >30% were used for subsequent sequencing library preparation to ensure data reliability. For six patients from MGH (Pt 35, Pt 42, Pt 208, Pt 272, Pt 530, Pt 98), RNA was purified from patients’ frozen or formalin-fixed tumor specimens using the Qiagen RNeasy Mini kit as previously described.42,90 For fresh frozen tumor samples and matched normal blood samples, DNA and RNA were extracted using the Qiagen AllPrep DNA/RNA Mini Kit (Cat# 80204, Qiagen; Germantown, MD, USA) according to the manufacturers’ instructions as previously described.20

sec.title: WES data acquisition and analysis
sec.p: WES data for patients Pt208, Pt42 and Pt98 were obtained from previously published study.20,37 All data generation methods, including library preparation with the Agilent SureSelect Human All Exon Kit v2 and sequencing on an Illumina HiSeq 2500 system, are detailed in the original publication.20,37 For this study, the raw sequencing data (FASTQ files) were re-analyzed. Briefly, data processing was performed using tools from the GATK suite (4.0.2.1) following GATK Best Practices guidelines. FASTQ files were aligned to the human reference genome (hg19) using BWA-MEM (0.7.17-r1188). Alignment attributes were restored with MergeBamAlignment, and PCR duplicates were marked using Picard MarkDuplicates (Version:2.25.1). Base quality score recalibration (BQSR) was conducted using BaseRecalibrator and ApplyBQSR.

Somatic mutations were identified by comparing tumor samples to their matched germline DNA using Mutect2 (in the GATK, v4.0.2.1) with default parameters. To construct phylogenetic trees depicting the evolutionary relationships between metastatic sites, the resulting variant call format (VCF) files were processed using Treeomics (v1.5.2) with its default settings.77

Loss of heterozygosity (LOH) were identified using VarScan (v2.3.9) with default parameters, and copy number variations (CNVs) were identified using sequenza (3.0.0) with default parameters. Gene-level copy number values were derived by mapping segmented CNV data to the genome annotation. Amplifications were defined as total copy number ≥4, and deletions were defined as total copy number ≤1. To analyze concurrent somatic mutations and deletions, we integrated the somatic variant calls from Mutect2 with the CNV data; a gene was classified as harboring concurrent events if it carried a non-synonymous mutation and was located within a chromosomal segment defined as a deletion. Furthermore, to specifically evaluate genomic alterations in the antigen presentation machinery, we performed a targeted analysis of MHC-related genes. The gene list was derived from the Molecular Signatures Database (MSigDB) (C2: Reactome collection), utilizing the REACTOME_MHC_CLASS_II_ANTIGEN_PRESENTATION and REACTOME_CLASS_I_MHC_MEDIATED_ANTIGEN_PROCESSING_PRESENTATION gene sets. For each sample, the CNV burden was quantified by calculating the number and fraction of genes within these sets that harbored somatic alterations, including amplifications, deletions, and LOH.

sec.title: RNA-seq data generation and analysis
sec.p: For six MGH patients (Pt 35, Pt 42, Pt 208, Pt 272, Pt 530, Pt 98), RNA libraries were prepared with 250 ng of RNA per fresh frozen sample using Qiagen AllPrepDNA/RNA Mini Kit (cat# 80204) following standard Illumina protocols.20 Sequencing was performed on the Illumina HiSeq 2000 (Broad Institute) and NextSeq 500 (Wistar Institute). Paired FASTQ files were aligned to the GRCh37 reference genome using the STAR aligner (version = 2.7.10a) with default settings. Read counts were summarized with featureCounts (2.0.3). Sequencing depths were normalized, and RPKMs (Reads Per Kilobase of transcript per Million mapped reads) were calculated using edgeR (3.32.1).

To correct for batch effects, ComBat-seq techniques were applied to raw read counts. The batch effect, a major technical variation between different datasets, was removed using the SVA R package ([3.38.0]) according to the COMBAT method.

Differential gene expression analysis was conducted using the limma package (3.46.0). ClusterProfiler (4.14.0) was used for downstream pathway enrichment analysis. Single-sample Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (ssGSEA) was applied using the GSVA package (1.38.2) with the HALLMARK gene set from MSigDB (v 6.1). Standard GSEA was implemented using the fgsea R package (1.16.0) with 10,000 permutations.

sec.title: NanoString nCounter Vantage 3D assays
sec.p: RNA and protein expression profiling from FFPE tissue was performed using the nCounter Vantage 3D RNA:Protein Solid Tumor Assay (Cat# VDRPC-SPKP-HSTF-12) following the manufacturer’s protocol. According to the product specifications, this assay enables multiplexed detection of 770 RNA targets (730 target genes and 40 housekeeping genes) and 27 total and phospho-proteins using antibody-oligonucleotide conjugates. The DNA SNV assay was prepared independently using the Vantage 3D DNA SNV Solid Tumor Panel, which contains 99 driver variants (comprising 5 technical replicates for 5 variants) from 25 genes that are frequently mutated in solid tumors, including SNV, multi-nucleotide variant (MNV), and insertions or deletions (InDels). For each sample, three FFPE sections (∼5 μm each) were allocated for DNA, RNA, and protein analysis, respectively. RNA and DNA were extracted directly from individual FFPE slides, whereas protein expression profiling was performed by in situ staining of FFPE sections with a DNA-barcoded antibody panel (Vantage 3D Solid Tumor Protein Panel). DNA barcodes were liberated by UV cleavage and collected for hybridization.

Hybridization reactions for RNA and protein were performed separately with their respective TagSets, after which the hybrids were pooled and loaded into a single nCounter cartridge lane for digital counting. The DNA SNV assay includes multiplex PCR enrichment of 104 predefined variants and subsequent hybridization with SNV-specific TagSets. All hybridized analytes were immobilized and imaged on the nCounter Analysis System to obtain digital fluorescent barcode counts, consistent with the workflow outlined in the product bulletin.

All datasets were processed using nSolver Analysis Software (v4.0) with the Advanced Analysis module. Technical quality control was performed using ERCC synthetic spike-in controls to assess hybridization performance and linearity. RNA sample quality was evaluated by the geometric mean of 40 reference genes. Protein QC was based on overall signal distribution and detection of expected targets.

RNA counts were normalized using positive control scaling followed by reference gene normalization based on the 40 housekeeping genes. Protein counts were normalized using the geometric mean of all detected protein targets within each sample. For SNV analysis, the nSolver SNV pipeline was applied with allele frequency thresholds set at 5% for variant detection.

Pathway activity estimation was performed using Principal Component Analysis (PCA) on Z-score-standardized, normalized RNA expression values. Pathways were defined according to the Hallmark gene sets (MSigDB v2023.2. Hs), and the first principal component of each gene set was used as the pathway activity score. PCA was conducted using the prcomp function in R (v4.3.1).

sec.title: EBtimecourse analysis
sec.p: To identify genes with dynamic expression patterns across longitudinal time points, the EBtimecourse R package (GitHub commit b87f017) was utilized. This package implements an empirical Bayes change-point model to detect significant changes in gene expression over time.84 Genes exhibiting temporal variation were identified at a false discovery rate (FDR) of less than 0.1. Genes were subsequently grouped based on their identified change points (i.e., the time point at which their expression changed) for visualization in heatmaps.

sec.title: RPPA and pathway activity analysis
sec.p: RPPA analysis was conducted at the RPPA Core Facility at The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center with 15mg–20mg of each fresh frozen sample.91 Tumor or cell lysates were serially diluted (five 2-fold dilutions, from undiluted to 1:16) and spotted onto nitrocellulose-coated slides in an 11 × 11 format using an arrayer. Slides were then probed with a panel of validated primary antibodies, and signals were amplified using a tyramide-based signal amplification system. Protein expression was visualized by a DAB (diaminobenzidine) colorimetric reaction.

Raw RPPA signal intensities were processed by the core facility using a standardized pipeline, which includes normalization for loading variation across samples. Data were processed using Replicates-Based Normalization (RBN) to mitigate batch effects, as detailed in Akbani et al.92 This resulted in a single, integrated dataset of relative protein levels.

For pathway analysis, these relative protein levels were median-centered and scaled by the standard deviation across all samples to obtain standardized Z-scores for each protein. Pathway activity scores were calculated based on the methodology established by Akbani et al.92 For each predefined pathway, a score was computed from the Z-scores of its member proteins. Specifically, the pathway score is the sum of the relative protein levels (Z-scores) of all positive regulatory components minus the Z-scores of negative regulatory components within that pathway. For proteins with multiple phosphorylation sites were measured separately.

sec.title: NanoString GeoMx DSP
sec.p: To quantify protein expression within spatially-defined compartments, we utilized the GeoMx DSP platform (NanoString Technologies) with the GeoMx Human Immuno-Oncology Protein Assay. The antibody panel includes 38 markers (33 functional, 5 structural/lineage). Single 5 μm FFPE slides from pre-treatment, on-treatment, and post-treatment immunotherapy samples were processed according to the manufacturer’s protocol. Briefly, slides were incubated with a multiplexed cocktail of primary antibodies conjugated to UV-photocleavable indexing oligonucleotides. Four fluorescent morphology markers (S100B, CD45, PanCK, DNA) were used for tissue visualization. Tissues were imaged on the GeoMx DSP instrument to generate high-resolution images. Regions of Interest (ROIs) were selected based on enrichment for melanocytic markers (S100B and Pmel17) and immune cell content (CD45 positivity) to assess immune infiltration. Each ROI was segmented into two Areas of Illumination (AOIs) to distinguish compartment-specific signaling: tumor (S100B/Pmel17 enriched) and immune (CD45 enriched). On average, 6 to 10 ROIs were analyzed per FFPE biopsy across 9 patients (except MGH Pt98). AOIs were sequentially exposed to UV light (365 nm) to release the indexing oligonucleotides, which were then collected and deposited into a microtiter plate. The collected oligonucleotides were hybridized to NanoString optical barcodes and quantified on the nCounter Analysis System. The raw protein expression data were generated and made accessible within the GeoMx DSP Analysis Suite (v2.1) for further processing.

After the readout data was imported, raw counts were sequentially normalized with positive control (ERCC) and geometrically averaged across all probes. For quality control, AOIs with fewer than 30 nuclei counts were excluded. The signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) was calculated using the geomean of control IgG counts (with a threshold set at 30 counts) and was used for further data analysis.

sec.title: CyCIF
sec.p: High-plex proteomic imaging was performed using cyclic immunofluorescence (CyCIF), with the detailed protocol adapted from previous work.43,44 Briefly, 5 μm FFPE slides underwent deparaffinization and antigen retrieval. Cells were then fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde for 30 min at room temperature, washed three times with PBS, and permeabilized in ice-cold methanol for 10 min. An initial image of the unstained slide was acquired to establish the baseline autofluorescence. The CyCIF process consisted of sequential rounds of antibody staining, imaging, and signal quenching. In each round, tissue sections were blocked in Odyssey blocking buffer (LI-COR) for 1 h at room temperature, then incubated with a cocktail of fluorescently-conjugated primary antibodies overnight at 4°C in blocking buffer. A complete list of antibodies, their clones, and suppliers is provided in Table S10. Following incubation, slides were washed three times with PBS and stained with a DNA counterstain 0.1 μg/mL Hoechst 33342 for 15 min at room temperature).

Slides were imaged at 10× magnification using a Zeiss Axioscan slide scanner. Following image acquisition, the fluorescent signal was quenched. This was achieved by incubating the slide for 1 h at room temperature with a solution of 3% H2O2 and 20 mM NaOH in PBS, under continuous illumination from a standard incandescent lamp. After quenching, slides were washed three times with PBS, and the cycle of blocking, staining, and imaging was repeated for the next set of antibodies.

Following acquisition, all images from a single slide were registered to correct for spatial shifts between cycles, using the Hoechst channel as a reference. This was performed using custom scripts in MATLAB (v2018b). The baseline autofluorescence image was then subtracted from each corresponding antibody image. Cell segmentation was performed using QI software (Quantitative Imaging Systems), defining individual cell boundaries based on the Hoechst nuclear signal. From each segmented cell, the mean protein intensity for all markers and the cell’s x/y coordinates were extracted to generate a single-cell expression matrix for further analysis. All data analysis was performed using custom Python scripts that are available on Github (https://github.com/biodev/cycIF-workflow/tree/v1.0).

sec.title: CyCIF clustering and spatial analysis
sec.p: After preprocessing, the protein expression matrix was used for further analysis. First, tumor cells, CD4+ T cells, Tregs, and macrophages were identified based on markers S100, CD4, CD45, CD68, and FOXP3 using the predict_phenotypes function from SPIAT (in R version 4.3.1).85 Next, tumor cells were further clustered using k-means clustering, accounting for pathway scores as outlined in Figure 4A. The first principal component (PC) of the protein expression in each pathway was used to represent the pathway score. Immune cells were clustered by the expression of Ki67 fitting a Gaussian mixture prediction model. We defined CIN (Cells in neighborhood) as the percentage of a target cell type within the 100 nearest neighbors. Tissue structures, including tumor borders, and the inside and outside regions, were also identified using the default settings of SPIAT.

sec.title: Integrated spatial analysis of CyCIF and DSP
sec.p: Image registration was performed in Fiji/ImageJ (version 1.54p) using a landmark-based affine transformation, with DAPI-stained nuclei serving as common fiducial markers for precise alignment. ROIs were excluded if they lacked histological annotation, could not be accurately registered to the corresponding CyCIF image due to tissue deformation, or contained fewer than 50 cells in the CyCIF map. A total of 126 ROIs profiled by DSP across 22 tissue sections were assessed for integration. Cellular composition within each quality-controlled DSP ROI was then quantified using CyCIF-derived single-cell segmentation and phenotyping data.

ROIs were stratified hierarchically to identify niches dominated by specific tumor subclones. First, an ROI was classified as “Tumor-Enriched” if >50% of its constituent cells were S100B+ tumor cells. Within this group, ROIs were further designated as subclone-specific niches based on the abundance of phenotypically distinct tumor cells. For example, a Tumor-Enriched ROI was defined as a “MITF+-High Niche” if the fraction of MITF+ tumor cells exceeded 25% of the total cells within that ROI. This same principle was applied to identify other key niches, such as those enriched for MITF−, AXL+, or Ki67+ tumor cells.

sec.title: Immune phenotyping in situ with mIHC
sec.p: Sequential IHC was performed on FFPE sections using an adapted protocol based on previously published methodologies.93,94 This assay utilized an 18-plex antibody panel designed to characterize major immune lineages (CD3 for T cells, CD20 for B cells, CD68 and CCR2 for monocytes/macrophages, CD66b for granulocytes, and HLA for APCs) and assess functional states (e.g., PD-1, EOMES, CD163, Granzyme B, Ki67) (Table S11). The study was conducted in two batches. In total, 160 Regions of Interest (ROIs) from 35 tumor samples, derived from 9 patients (3 Rs, 6 NRs), were assayed, yielding data from over 7.1 million cells. Briefly, slides were deparaffinized and stained with hematoxylin (S330130-2, Agilent, Santa Clara, CA), followed by whole-slide scanning at 20× magnification using an Aperio AT2 scanner (Leica Biosystems, Wetzlar, Germany). The tissues then underwent 15 min of heat-mediated antigen retrieval in pH 6.0 Citra solution (BioGenex, Fremont, CA), followed by 10 min of blocking with Dako Dual Endogenous Enzyme Block (S2003, Dako, Santa Clara, CA), and another 10 min of protein blocking using 5% normal goat serum and 2.5% BSA in TBST. A specific primary antibody, as outlined in Table S11, was then applied and incubated overnight at 4°C. After washing off the primary antibody with TBST, either anti-rat, anti-mouse, or anti-rabbit Histofine Simple Stain MAX PO HRP-conjugated polymer (Nichirei Biosciences, Tokyo, Japan) was applied for 30 min at room temperature, followed by development with AEC chromogen (Vector Laboratories, Burlingame, CA). Slides were digitally scanned after each chromogen development. HRP inactivation was performed by incubating the slides for 10 min with Dako Dual Endogenous Enzyme Block (S2003, Dako, Santa Clara, CA). This inactivation step was performed between staining rounds, allowing for the application of primary antibodies from another species after another protein-blocking step, as described above. Between cycles, heat mediated antigen retrieval was used (pH6 citrate) to elute primary antibodies from tissues in order to prepare for the next cycle (containing up to three rounds). Note, HRP block was not necessary prior to hematoxylin staining.

Scanned images were registered in MATLAB version R2018b using the SURF algorithm in the Computer Vision Toolbox (The MathWorks, Inc., Natick, MA). Image processing, segmentation and cell quantification were performed using Fiji (ImageJ version 1.54p),68 CellProfiler Version 3.5.1,95 and FCS Express 7 Image Cytometry RUO (De Novo Software, Glendale, CA). AEC signal was extracted for quantification and visualization in FIJI using a custom macro for color deconvolution. Briefly, the FIJI plugin Color_Deconvolution [H AEC] was used to separate hematoxylin, followed by postprocessing steps for signal cleaning and background elimination. AEC signal was extracted in FIJI using with the NIH plugin RGB_to_CMYK. Color deconvoluted images were processed in CellProfiler to quantify single cell mean intensity signal measurements for every stained marker. Cell profiler outputs were loaded into FCS image cytometry gating software, and hierarchical gating was carried out as shown in Figure S7B.

sec.title: TLS identification and assessment
sec.p: TLSs were identified and quantified using the mIHC whole-slide images based on methods previously described.96 Specifically, the spatial distribution of CD20+ B cells was evaluated in conjunction with CD3+ T cells to map lymphoid aggregates. In accordance with established criteria, TLSs were defined as dense immune cell aggregates containing more than 50 CD20+ B cells.

To complement the mIHC assessment, we further evaluated TLS status using NanoString GeoMx DSP data. A TLS gene signature score was calculated for each ROI using a panel of key lymphocyte and checkpoint markers comprising CD3, CD4, CD8, CD20, and PD-1, based on the gene set derived from identifying super-resolution tissue architecture.97 In accordance with the scoring methodology described by Cabrita et al., the TLS score was defined as the mean normalized expression of these signature genes.48

sec.title: DC-associated MHC class II enriched region identification and score assessment
sec.p: In our mIHC panel (Batch 1), DCs were phenotypically defined as CD45+CD3−CD20−CD66b−CD68−CCR2−HLA-II+CD11c+. We spatially quantified the fraction of CD4+ and CD8+ T cells located within a 60-μm radius of these identified DCs. To characterize this antigen-presenting architecture within the DSP dataset, we established a “DC-associated MHC class II score”. This score was defined as the mean normalized expression of representative markers for DCs, T cells, and antigen presentation, specifically HLA-DR, CD11c, CD3, CD4 and CD8.

sec.title: Recurrent cellular neighborhoods (RCNs) analysis in mIHC
sec.p: RCNs were quantified to evaluate the spatial organization of tissue. For each cell, a neighborhood was defined by counting all cells within a 60-μm radius of the seed cell’s center, based on previous studies.46 These neighborhoods were then clustered using k-means, with cell proportions serving as the features. The elbow method was employed to determine the optimal number of clusters, which revealed groups of spatially similar neighborhoods across all ROIs.

sec.title: Spatial analysis of cell-cell interactions
sec.p: To investigate the spatial arrangement of cells within the TME, we utilized the spatial context-preserving capabilities of mIHC. We evaluated interactions between two distinct cell states by measuring their proximity within a 20-μm radius, following the approach outlined in previous studies.47 To minimize bias from abundant cell states, we normalized the total cell-cell interactions by dividing the combined densities of the interacting cell states.

sec.title: 10x Genomics Visium HD library preparation
sec.p: Spatial transcriptomic analysis was performed using the 10x Genomics Visium HD Spatial Gene Expression platform. Services were provided by Gaojing (Zhejiang Anji) Precision Medicine Technology Co., Ltd. Briefly, FFPE tumor samples (Patient S002; pre- and post-anti-PD-1) with RNA quality scores of DV200 > 30% were selected (measured by Agilent 2100 Bioanalyzer). 5μm thick tissue sections were mounted onto a Visium HD Gene Expression slide (10x Genomics), baked at 42°C for 3 h, and dried overnight. To initiate deparaffinization, the slides were incubated at 60°C for 2 h, immersed in xylene, and rehydrated using a graded ethanol series. H&E staining was performed with Mayer’s hematoxylin (Millipore Sigma), bluing reagent (Dako, Agilent), and alcoholic eosin (Millipore Sigma). The stained slides were then scanned under a microscope before proceeding with decrosslinking using 0.1N HCl and TE buffer (pH 9.0) to release formalin-sequestered RNA. Following decrosslinking, the slides were incubated with a human whole transcriptome probe panel (10x Genomics), which was subsequently transferred to the Cytassist system (10x Genomics). This probe panel consists of three pairs of specific probes: one pair at the 5′ end containing Small RNA Read 2S, and one pair at the 3′ end containing poly-A sequences. These probes were hybridized to the RNA in the tissue. The probe pairs were ligated to seal the junctions, creating single-stranded ligation products. To facilitate the capture of RNA, the samples were treated with RNase and permeabilized to release the ligation products. The poly-A portion of the ligation products was captured by the poly(dT) regions of capture probes precoated on the Visium slide. These capture probes also contained Illumina Read 1 sequences, spatial barcodes, and unique molecular identifiers (UMIs).

The ligated probe products were spatially barcoded, extended, and then released from the slide for indexing via Sample Index PCR. Finally, libraries were constructed and sequenced using Illumina paired-end sequencing (NovaSeq X Plus), with 16-bp spatial barcodes and 12-bp UMIs encoded in Read 1. The ligated probe inserts were sequenced using Read 2S.

sec.title: Visium HD spatial sequencing data analysis
sec.p: After sequencing, the reads were aligned to the Visium Human Transcriptome Probe Set v2.0, and the expression matrix was extracted using the Space Ranger pipeline. To reconstruct the single-cell expression matrix from the 2-μm bin output of Space Ranger, we used Bin2Cell (version 0.3.0),50 which utilizes StarDist for segmentation. For cell type annotation, we used the machine learning tool CellTypist (version 1.6.3), which was applied using scRNA-seq data downloaded from GSE186344, where three BrM samples were available.51 Cells with a confidence score greater than 0.1 were retained for further analysis. The Seurat v5 package was then employed to analyze the expression matrix. The data was then normalized using the logNormalization function. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) was performed on the scaled data, harmony (version 1.2.3) was used to integrate data from different samples, and UMAP was calculated for visualization. Cell-cell interactions were calculated as described earlier. Lastly, CellChat (version 1.6.1) was used to perform cell-cell communication analysis, quantifying secreted signaling interactions from CellChatDB. R package ‘nichenetr’ (version 2.2.1.1) was used to explore whether specific ligands in stroma could contribute to the upregulation of the malignant ‘c1’ signature.

sec.title: Coordinate-based image registration of mIHC and CyCIF
sec.p: To integrate the spatial organization of RCNs (defined by mIHC) with the high-dimensional protein expression profiles from CyCIF, we performed landmark-based image registration using the BigWarp plugin in Fiji/ImageJ. Corresponding anatomical landmarks were manually selected as control points (coordinate pairs) in both the mIHC (moving) and CyCIF (fixed) images. Coordinates were extracted from the ROI Manager to facilitate precise single-cell alignment across modalities. Subsequently, tissue regions were tessellated into 200 × 200 μm spatial grids. Each grid was assigned to a specific RCN phenotype if it met the following criteria: (1) it contained >50 cells in the CyCIF dataset, and (2) >50% of the mIHC-defined cells within the grid belonged to that specific RCN. Finally, differential tumor cell expression profiles were compared between RCN3-enriched and RCN1-enriched grids using the CyCIF data.

sec.title: Validation of the tumor mTOR signature in public cohorts
sec.p: For validation by bulk RNA-seq analysis, gene expression data (RSEM) and clinical information for the TCGA-SKCM cohort were obtained from the GDC Data Portal (https://portal.gdc.cancer.gov/, Level 3). Expression matrices (TPM) and clinical data for the Riaz et al., Du et al., Auslander et al., and Gide et al. cohorts were downloaded from the GEO database.41,42,57,58 In these bulk datasets, the tumor mTOR signature was defined as the combination of the melanoma-specific gene (TYRP2) and mTOR signaling pathway genes derived from REACTOME (v6.1).

For validation by single-cell analysis, we re-analyzed scRNA-seq count data from Quek et al.(https://doi.org/10.17632/w55dvbb82f.1), specifically focusing on matched pre- and post-treatment samples from patient MIA11.33 Data were processed using the Seurat pipeline. Low-quality cells (detected genes <200 or >6,000; mitochondrial reads >20%) were excluded. Data were normalized, scaled, and subjected to PCA, followed by batch correction using Harmony. Dimensionality reduction was performed using UMAP, and clusters were identified using a shared nearest neighbor (SNN) modularity optimization-based clustering algorithm. Cell types were annotated based on representative marker expression identified using the FindAllMarkers function. For mTOR signature analysis in the single cell level, mTOR signatures only included mTOR signaling genes from REACTOME (v6.1), and signature score was calculated using ‘AddModule’ function. Tumor cells were re-clustered into subtypes using default parameters. Tumor clusters ranking in the top 3 for mTOR signature scores were defined as “mTOR-high clusters”. The differential abundance of mTOR-high clusters between pre- and post-treatment samples was calculated by Fisher’s exact test.

sec.title: Definition of the RCN3 score
sec.p: Naive CD8+ T cell signatures were defined by classical markers (CD8A, TCF7, LEF1, SELL, CCR7), while effector CD8+ T cell signatures included CD8A and PDCD1. Corresponding scores were calculated using ssGSEA. The RCN3 score was defined as follows:

sec.title: Survival analysis of mTOR and RCN3 signatures
sec.p: To evaluate Overall Survival (OS) in the TCGA and Du et al. cohorts.,36,41 survival curves were fitted using the Kaplan-Meier method with the R package survival (v3.1-12) and visualized using the ggsurvplot function in survminer (v0.4.9). Patients were stratified into high- and low-expression groups based on the median values of the tumor mTOR or RCN3 signature scores.

sec.title: External validation of the c1 signature
sec.p: To validate the malignant ‘c1’ signature, marker genes were identified using the FindMarkers function (logFC >0.5, p < 0.01), and signature scores were calculated using the AddModuleScore function. We utilized two external scRNA-seq cohorts: Yang et al. (GSE26993632)32 and Sade-Feldman et al. (GSE120575).25 Data processing (i.e., quality control, integration, clustering, cell annotation, and scoring) of Yang et al. cohort was performed using the same pipeline described for the Quek et al. cohort. For the Sade-Feldman cohort, analysis was restricted to cells annotated as “G8-Cytotoxicity Lymphocytes” based on the original publication.

sec.title: Quantification and statistical analysis
sec.p: Statistical analyses were performed using two-sided Student’s t-tests unless otherwise specified, with p < 0.05 considered statistically significant. Differential expression between groups was assessed using two-sided Student’s t-tests applied to log2-transformed normalized counts, with significance defined as |log2 fold-change| > 1 and p < 0.05. All statistical analyses were conducted in R (v4.3.1) unless otherwise stated.

Exact sample sizes (n), definitions of biological versus technical replicates, specific statistical tests used for each experiment, and criteria for sample inclusion or exclusion are provided in the corresponding figure legends. Where applicable, data distributions were assessed for normality, and appropriate parametric or non-parametric tests were applied. Center values represent means unless noted otherwise, and error bars indicate standard error of the mean (SEM). No statistical methods were used to predetermine sample size, and analyses were not performed blind unless otherwise indicated.

list-item.p: All data generated or analyzed in this study have been deposited in publicly accessible repositories or provided in the supplemental information. WES data of Pt98, Pt42, and Pt208 are available from dbGaP (phs001427.v2.p1).20,37 RNA-seq data of MGH patients were obtained through the GEO database under accession codes GEO: GSE115821, GSE168204, and GSE273583. The raw sequencing data of GEO: GSE273583 are available in the Sequence Read Archive (SRA) under BioProject accession number SRA: PRJNA1142462 (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/bioproject/PRJNA1142462). RNA-seq data from Johnson et al. were obtained from the corresponding author.39 RNA-seq data from the Lee et al. cohort are available in the EGA database under accession code EGAD00001005738.38 For patients S001 and S002, nCounter RNA, nCounter protein, and DSP data are available in Zenodo under https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.18458128 (https://zenodo.org/records/18458128). Data for the remaining patients including nCounter RNA, nCounter protein, and DSP results are available in GEO under accessions GEO: GSE317937, GSE317936, and GSE318248, respectively. SNV data for patients MP13_674 and G001 are available in GEO under GEO: GSE317918. RPPA data for Pt42 and Pt208 are available under GEO: GSE317912. CyCIF and mIHC image data are archived in Zenodo under https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.14899123 (https://zenodo.org/records/14899123). Normalized nCounter RNA (Table S4), normalized nCounter protein (Table S5), processed RPPA (Table S7), and DSP (Table S9) data are provided in the supplemental information. The 10× Genomics Visium HD data generated in this study have been deposited in the Genome Sequence Archive (GSA) at the Beijing Institute of Genomics (BIG) Data Center (https://ngdc.cncb.ac.cn/gsa-human/), under BioProject Accession PRJCA036416 (https://ngdc.cncb.ac.cn/bioproject/browse/PRJCA036416) (accession number HRA010486, https://ngdc.cncb.ac.cn/gsa-human/browse/HRA010486).

The main R scripts used for data processing are available on https://github.com/Liulab/longitudinal_multiomics_melanoma_ICB_resistance or can be requested from Y.D. No custom code was generated in this study.
Any additional information required to reanalyze the data reported in this paper is available from the lead contact upon request.
